societies.name: Star Trek — Mudd’s android-serviced captivity
societies.society: Harry Mudd’s existing supported residence on the android planet

scope.period: Mudd’s established residence before the Enterprise escape and android reprogramming
scope.population: Harry Mudd, the resident living human receiving android service
exclusions: Temporary Enterprise captives as a stable resident population
The unimplemented plan to control humanity
Post-reprogramming parole as an identical political system

societies.description:
Mudd already lives among androids that supply personal services and productive support after their makers have died. The retained unit is his narrow existing residence, not the machines’ proposed expansion across human civilization. His support does not depend on a wage or an outside human household staff. That gives the arrangement a strong material-guarantee estimate within its tiny scope. Captivity is a major restriction on freedom, but refusal to let him leave does not itself prove that food or care is withheld.

Mudd presents himself as a ruler, yet the androids can reject his commands and prevent his departure. Their coordinated machine authority therefore matters more than his imperial title when estimating effective control. This point lies toward autonomous AI provision, with uncertainty about the exact mixture of accepted requests and binding restrictions. Personal enjoyment, manipulation and confinement do not provide a trustworthy work census, so the participation axis remains unresolved. The crew’s later reprogramming changes the arrangement and is not silently treated as the same authority structure.

guarantees.basis: Existing android service supports the sole human resident without a wage; confinement is distinguished from demonstrated withdrawal of material care.

control.basis: The android network overrides Mudd’s wishes, including departure, despite his apparent command over many personal services.

nonworking.basis: The resident’s activities are not a stable all-purpose labor census; no exact leisure fraction is supplied.

evidence.claim: Mudd already receives android service, but the machines refuse to permit his departure.
evidence.locator: Episode/reference pre-escape residence and android agenda

uncertainties: A single-human continuing support unit, explicitly limited in size.
Mudd’s title is not effective productive ownership.
Only the pre-reprogramming authority is scored.
Promises to serve humanity at large are not an enacted economy.

review.method: Second pass against the gathered passages, including explicit uncertainty; no independent reviewer

societies.name: Star Trek — Aldea under the Custodian
societies.society: Aldean residents supported by the Custodian

scope.period: Established Custodian provision before the defense-system shutdown and technical relearning
scope.population: Living biological Aldean residents, used as a humanoid-person comparison proxy
exclusions: Kidnapped Enterprise children as a stable separate society

societies.description:
Aldea has a direct technological support system: the Custodian supplies residents’ needs while recommending pursuits such as the arts. Ordinary provision is therefore materially separated from necessary production jobs. The guarantee estimate is strong for residents, but it does not imply perfect health protection. The planetary defenses have damaging environmental effects, and the population has lost the knowledge needed to diagnose the resulting infertility. The scope is the existing Aldean community before its systems are changed. Biological humanoid residents are an explicit comparison proxy for the human-centered axes.

Residents can command the Custodian through personal interfaces, and its access clearances show structured humanlike participation rather than an unquestionable AI sovereign. The broad positive control estimate reflects dispersed practical access, while leaving uncertainty about elite privileges and the ability to alter underlying infrastructure. Lack of engineering knowledge is a vulnerability, not sufficient proof that the machine owns everything. Artistic study and other chosen activity can still be useful work, so automatic provision does not justify a numerical nonworking share. Later technical relearning is not projected backward into this period.

guarantees.basis: Resident needs are supplied by a continuing system, but environmentally induced infertility and lost maintenance knowledge qualify its health/security floor.

control.basis: Residents have command interfaces and clearances, but the reference does not fully establish collective ownership or the distribution of privileged access.

nonworking.basis: Recommended artistic study and chosen useful pursuits do not yield an all-person participation census.

evidence.claim: The Custodian provides needs, accepts resident commands and recommends studies while the defense system damages the environment.

uncertainties: Explicit biological humanoid-person proxy, not an undocumented human population.
Fan reference evidence remains provisional and is one chain rather than independent corroboration.
Control is broad and uncertain; resident command is not automatically common legal ownership.
Kidnapping and the later intervention are not additional settled societies.

review.method: Second pass against the gathered passages, including explicit uncertainty; no independent reviewer

decisions.reason: Sleeper’s domestic robots do not establish the police state’s general material-access system.
decisions.analysis: A poet’s purchased servant and instant food preparation show sectoral and domestic automation, not population-wide work independence.

decisions.reason: Computerized war and disintegration obligations do not establish a post-work production and distribution mechanism.
decisions.analysis: The treaty concerns lethal casualty compliance rather than access to ordinary material goods.

decisions.reason: Landru’s behavioral control does not establish Beta III’s automatic material provision.
decisions.analysis: The Body and Red Hour describe coercion and social regulation; no household economy is supplied by the short check.
decisions.follow_up: Skip a full episode transcript or lore reconstruction.

decisions.reason: Vaal’s village has supplies and machine authority, but the automatic-production and allocation mechanism remains unclear.
decisions.analysis: Food, hospitality and restrictions do not themselves show a durable weakening of labor’s role in acquiring necessities.
decisions.follow_up: Skip further episode reading; do not erase villagers’ real servicing activity.

decisions.reason: The Oracle’s navigation and religious authority do not establish Yonada’s household provisioning rules.
decisions.analysis: An automatic worldship can contain different human labor and allocation systems. Licensed-novel backstory is separately marked and not adopted.

decisions.reason: Mudd’s existing android-supported residence has actual provision and effective machine authority despite his title.
Triskelion’s thralls perform real entertainment labor for biological Providers.
decisions.analysis: Captivity, alien brains and advanced machines do not by themselves establish a post-work material-access order.
decisions.follow_up: Keep as an alien exploitation comparison without equating biological rulers with AI.

decisions.reason: Exo III’s surviving android machinery does not establish a supported extant human community.
decisions.analysis: Dead creators do not enter a leisure denominator, and later research or human-derived copies do not establish a general economic constitution.

decisions.reason: The Eymorg’s brain-controlled infrastructure does not have verified household allocation in the short check.
decisions.analysis: A stolen living brain performs a real controlling function; it must not be relabeled as an external autonomous AI merely because it interfaces with machinery.
decisions.follow_up: Skip transcript reconstruction; reopen only for a clear provision account.

decisions.reason: The Custodian explicitly provides residents’ needs while accepting resident commands, with the alien-person proxy and uncertain governance disclosed.
Borg drones perform useful human-derived and biological cyborg labor rather than becoming a passive nonworking population.
decisions.analysis: Collective computation, assimilation and maintenance remain actual work. Cybernetic control is not sufficient evidence that robots replaced the persons’ contribution.
decisions.follow_up: Keep as an embodied collective-labor comparison.

decisions.reason: Bynar dependence on a master computer does not establish work-independent household access.
decisions.analysis: Cybernetic life support and networked thought can coexist with real work and different property systems.

review_notes: Twelve reference-led decisions, two bounded admissions; no complete episode transcript read or viewing.
Mudd’s existing single-human support unit is distinct from an unrealized plan to capture all humanity and the later reprogrammed parole.
Aldea accepts resident commands; AI provision does not itself imply AI sovereignty. The biological alien proxy is explicit.
Unrelated Landru-name hits, a wiki talk-page opinion and Star Trek band material were discarded; licensed-novel Oracle history is not screen canon.
